What Is a Force?: A force is a push or a pull. It has size and direction, so it is a vector, and its SI unit is the newton (N). The net force is the sum of all forces on an object, adding forces in the same direction and subtracting opposite ones. Balanced forces have a net force of zero and do not change the motion. Unbalanced forces make the object accelerate. A free-body diagram shows all the forces on one object with arrows.
Newton's First Law: Inertia: Newton's first law says that an object at rest stays at rest and an object in motion keeps moving at constant velocity in a straight line unless an unbalanced force acts on it. This tendency is called inertia, and an object's mass measures its inertia: more mass means more inertia. Seat belts, sliding on ice and a tablecloth trick all show inertia. Friction is the unbalanced force that makes things on Earth stop.
Newton's Second Law: F = ma: Newton's second law says that the acceleration of an object is equal to the net force divided by its mass: a = F / m, or F = ma. The acceleration points in the direction of the net force. For a given force a larger mass gives a smaller acceleration, and for a given mass a larger force gives a larger acceleration. One newton is the force that gives a 1 kg mass an acceleration of 1 m/s^2. Combine with v = v_i + a t to find the speed after a time.
Newton's Third Law: Newton's third law says that when one object exerts a force on a second object, the second object exerts an equal force in the opposite direction on the first. The two forces are an action-reaction pair. They are equal in size, opposite in direction, act at the same time and act on different objects, so they never cancel each other. Rockets, swimming and walking all depend on this law. The accelerations can differ because the masses differ, a = F / m.
Gravity, Weight and Friction: Gravity is the attraction between masses. Weight is the force of gravity on an object, W = mg, measured in newtons, while mass is the amount of matter and stays the same everywhere. On Earth g is 9.8 m/s^2 and on the Moon about 1.6 m/s^2. Friction is a force that opposes motion between surfaces. Static friction acts on objects that are not moving, sliding friction on objects that slide and rolling friction on rolling objects. Friction depends on the surfaces and on how hard they are pressed together. Air resistance is a form of fluid friction, and at terminal velocity the net force is zero.
